Jean Buxton (holding her water bottle) and two Mandari men sitting in the covered back of a Land Rover during her fieldwork. It is possible that this image was taken by Godfrey Lienhardt who visited Buxton during her fieldwork in 1950.
A portrait of a European, probably English, woman, standing at the entrance to a Mandari hut.

A portrait of a European, probably English, woman sitting on a low stool and leaning on a wooden planter under a large fringed sunshade. She is probably the wife of a local colonial administrator, one of whom (Paul Howell) Buxton was a cousin to.

Two dogs looking out of a truck in Mandari, probably the pets of local colonial administrators that Jean Buxton spent time with during her fieldwork. One local administrator, the anthropologist Paul Howell, was a cousin of Buxton's.

An unidentified European couple in their home, in an unknown location. The photograph has been posed by Buxton in the manner of an 'interiors' magazine, with both the husband and wife adopting stereotyped gender positions within the home space in keeping with 1950s English society. It is evident however that at least some of the intention of the image is to show off the colonial lifestyle, with modern civilised living indoors coupled with relaxing outdoor living in the warmth, the two dimensions of colonial life flowing between each other unhindered through the large wall opening.

The interior of an unidentified colonial home, possibly in Kenya or Uganda, although it is uncertain when or if Buxton visited either country. The central subject of the image is the modernist display cabinet set against the interior wall which incorporates a series of apertures, two of which incorporate windows, into which selected works of African art have been inserted for display. To the right of the display a conventional oil painting of an English landscape hangs on the wall.
